Lack of oxygen in the morning
Khắc phục nhiệt độ bể cá cảnh tăng cao ngày hè
[Kiến thức] Tất tần tật về cách tạo oxy cho cá không cần máy
Hướng Dẫn Chi Tiết Cách Tăng Oxy Cho Bể Cá Cảnh Khỏe Mạnh - Aquatech

facts.fact: Dissolved oxygen is O2 gas held in water. Fish and other aquatic animals need it because they cannot use the oxygen bound in water molecules (H2O).
Dissolved oxygen comes from photosynthesis by plants and algae, and from the air by diffusion. Wind, waves and mechanical aerators speed up the diffusion.
Cooler water holds more oxygen. Water at 90°F holds about 7.4 mg/L and water at 45°F about 11.9 mg/L.
Warm-water fish in Florida generally need about 5 ppm (5 mg/L) of dissolved oxygen for good health. Below about 2 mg/L, fish become stressed.
A dissolved oxygen level above 5 mg/L is optimal for most finfish. Fish are stressed below 5 mg/L, and deaths may occur at 4 mg/L or less, depending on the species and how long they are exposed.
Aquarium Co-Op says a freshwater tank should ideally have about 7 to 8 ppm (mg/L) of dissolved oxygen.
Aquatech says about 4.5 to 8 mg/L is ideal for most freshwater ornamental fish, that some sensitive or cold-water species need more, and that below 3 mg/L is dangerous and can kill many fish.
Oxygen is plentiful on sunny days, when photosynthesis peaks, and falls after sunset. Fish kills often happen around 4 to 6 am, just before dawn.
Dissolved oxygen is lowest in the early morning, but low levels can happen at any time.
In an aquarium, an oxygen saturation below 100% may mean the aeration is not enough for the bioload.
Gas exchange at the water surface lets carbon dioxide leave and oxygen dissolve in, and surface agitation improves it.
Fish short of oxygen gather near the surface and gulp air, which is called "piping". Hypoxia causes sudden, heavy deaths that are usually noticed early in the morning.
Large fish are affected by low oxygen more than small fish.
Piping can also be caused by high nitrite or gill disease, not only by low dissolved oxygen. Nitrite poisoning gives chocolate-brown gills (brown blood disease).
A typical sign is fish staying near the surface in the morning, gasping, then swimming normally soon after the lights come on.
Brief gasping after a meal is normal and should stop about an hour later.
JBL says many reported oxygen problems turn out to be nitrite problems, usually from overstocking or a damaged bacterial culture.
Fish short of oxygen may rest on the bottom, lose their appetite and move their gills rapidly. In the worst cases they gasp at the surface.
Other signs of low oxygen are rapid breathing, sluggishness, fish gathering near filter outlets or air stones, loss of colour, refusing food, and more disease.
Fish short of oxygen swim slowly and eat poorly. They hang at the surface with the head up to breathe and the tail sunk.
At night, oxygen in an aquarium can fall well below 4 mg/l, especially after heavy use during the day.
Dense planting, especially over 70% of the floor area, can cause a lack of oxygen at night, because plants use oxygen in the dark.
Natural decorations such as roots and leaves can lower oxygen, because bacteria use oxygen as they break them down.
Heavy algae growth, or algae dying off suddenly, lowers oxygen by feeding bacterial breakdown.
Bacteria breaking down ammonia and nitrite use more oxygen after cleaning, after a disturbance, and while a new tank is running in.
Care products, medications, anti-algae products and some filter media can lower oxygen by killing algae or disturbing bacteria.
JBL names overstocking with fish and too few plants as the most common causes of low oxygen.
Other causes of low oxygen are cloudy weather, an algal bloom dying, overfeeding, overstocking and uncleaned old ponds.
Warm water speeds up the fish's metabolism as well as holding less oxygen, so fish use oxygen faster.
Other causes of low oxygen are a still water surface, too many fish, decaying organic waste, overdosing medicines or chemicals, and power cuts or broken equipment.
A failed or dirty filter, polluted water, and too many fish and plants can cause a lack of oxygen.
For a quick fix when oxygen is low, do a large water change to bring in fresh oxygen, then look for the cause.

Aquatech's emergency steps are to stir the surface gently by hand for 5–10 minutes, repeated every 30–60 minutes; to run a battery air pump; to change about 20–30% of the water; or to move some fish to a prepared spare tank.
JBL OxyTabs are only for short-term needs, such as moving fish, and are not a lasting fix.
To raise oxygen, set the filter outlet just below the surface and angle it diagonally upward so it moves the surface.
An air pump with a diffuser run during the dark hours adds oxygen. JBL names the JBL PROSILENT a200 and the filter diffuser JBL VenturiSet 12/16.
For a lasting fix, remove the cause: dead plant parts, algae, sludge and rotting spots, plus any decorations or products added recently.
The JBL PROAQUATEST O2 kit is used by adding 2 x 6 drops of reagent and comparing the colour to a chart. The result takes about 30 seconds.

JBL advises testing oxygen weekly before water changes. When there is a problem, test half an hour before lights on, at least 3 hours after lights on, half an hour before lights off, and at least 3 hours after lights off.
To set up an air stone you need an air pump, airline tubing, and a check valve to stop water flowing back into the tubing.
A long, shallow tank has more surface area for gas exchange than a tall, narrow one.
Do not let floating plants cover the whole water surface.
Aquarium Co-Op recommends at least one air source, such as an air stone or sponge filter, in every aquarium.
Aquatech suggests keeping backup power, such as a generator or UPS, keeping filters clean, keeping the temperature stable, and changing about 20–30% of the water every week or two.
Aquatic plants add oxygen by day but use it at night, so they should not be a tank's only oxygen source.
A common mistake is watching only oxygen and ignoring ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, pH and temperature.
A common mistake is confusing oxygen with CO2 in planted tanks. Too much CO2 can lower both oxygen and pH.
Adding too many aeration devices can stress fish and make noise without adding much oxygen.
Feeding fish during a power cut is a mistake, because leftover food uses up extra oxygen.
Turning a filter back on after a power cut without cleaning it first sends toxins from the filter back into the tank.
Tepbac, a Vietnamese site, says hot summer weather raises aquarium water temperature, and warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cool water, so fish can struggle to breathe or suffocate.
Tepbac gives about 24–28°C as the ideal aquarium water temperature.
For hot days, Tepbac suggests a gentle fan blowing across the water surface, a partly open lid or a mesh cover, ice only in a sealed bag, and a chiller as the most effective long-term option.
Tepbac advises partial water changes in the early morning or evening, with the new water within about 2°C of the tank.
Thế Giới Cá Cảnh, a Vietnamese shop, names power cuts that stop the air pump as a cause of low oxygen.
Without an air pump, Thế Giới Cá Cảnh suggests a foot pump attached to airline tubing and an airstone, run for a few minutes, or stirring the water by hand or with a stick.
Aquatech, a Vietnamese shop, says that in a power cut a tank may last from a few hours to about a day, depending on its size and stocking, and recommends a battery air pump as backup.
